newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal gears up for pension reform.
newsitem.headline: Portugal gears up for pension reform.

text.p: Portugal's pension funds are set for spectacular growth into the 21st century and the creaking social security system is gearing up for reform, industry and government officials say.
As in many other countries, Portugal will have to support a greater number of retired people as birthrates fall and people live longer.
"The social security system has begun to suffer from financial disequilibrium linked to the ageing population," Employment Minister Maria Joao Rodrigues told Reuters.
The Portuguese, who have traditionally depended heavily on the state for their pensions, are now turning increasingly to private savings plans to pay for longer retirements.
"I think individuals rather than firms will save much more in private pension plans," said Jose Manuel Mendinhos, a former head of the Association of Pension Fund Managers.
The effort to save in private schemes will be hard for a people whose disposable income is among the lowest in Europe and who already struggle to meet social security commitments.
The average state pension in Portugal is around 30,000 escudos ($190) per month, officials said.

Mendinhos, who is managing director of Futuro, a company that invests and manages occupational and private pension funds, said he did not expect many private companies to start their own pension schemes in the coming years.
Mendinhos estimated that just one in a thousand Portuguese firms presently operated their own occupational pension scheme.
Futuro manages the retirement savings of employees of state utility EDP-Electricidade de Portugal, oil company Petrogal, airport company ANA as well as private firms and individuals.
Mendinhos said he expected pension funds to boost investments in Portuguese shares in the coming months as returns outstripped declining bond yields.
A surge in share buying by pension funds could give a big lift to a small bourse like Lisbon, industry officials said.
In the third quarter of 1996, shares accounted for just 10 percent of the total investment of Portuguese pension funds, while bonds represented 70 percent, according to the latest industry figures.
Property accounted for five percent, foreign investments, mainly shares, five percent, and other investments including cash 10 percent.
Industry officials said they doubted the government would impose restrictions on share investments by pension funds as any measures to limit returns would hurt both savers and funds.
